speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, the impact on our industries has been uneven.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Minister Lim Hng Kiang has just spoken on the external headwinds that are affecting industries, such as wholesale trade and marine and offshore engineering, as well as the weakness in industries, such as food services and real estate.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Nonetheless, there are other industries, such as information and communications, education, and health and social services, where demand remains resilient.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has asked about business costs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The cost of utilities is expected to remain subdued, given sustained low oil prices.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And there are similar trends for those in the industry, especially because they have greater flexibility in negotiating contracts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And the strong pipeline supply of industrial and commercial space coming on-stream in 2016 should continue to ease rental cost pressures.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For labour costs, there are variations across sectors.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In the manufacturing sector, unit labour cost (ULC) fell by 0.7%.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is in Q2 on a year-on-year basis on the back of productivity improvements.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In contrast, the ULC in the services sector rose by 4.5%.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These trends, and their differential impact on our industries, underscore the need to redouble our efforts to improve productivity and to adopt industry-specific strategies to sustain competitiveness.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Against this challenging economic backdrop, the Government seeks to help companies manage immediate pressures but also importantly to adapt to stay competitive in the medium to long term.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, SPRINGSingapore launched the Working Capital Loan (WCL) this year to help address Small and Medium Enterprises' (SMEs) near-term cash flow concerns and growth financing needs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This year, there has been a strong take-up of SPRINGSingapore's various loan schemes, with over S$1.2 billion worth of loans given to SMEs so far.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Notwithstanding these cyclical headwinds, there remain good market opportunities for our companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If I can illustrate, the annual growth for the ASEAN region is expected to average 5.2% from 2016 to 2020.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, for Asia, it is meant to be even higher.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And this is significantly higher, compared to the projected global growth for the same period.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To seize these opportunities, our industries, enterprises and workers must transform.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Structurally, Singapore is entering a new mode of growth.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Rather than increasing manpower, we must anchor Singapore's competitiveness and growth in increased productivity and greater innovation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, in April this year, the Government announced a grant budget of over S$2.3 billion under the Enterprise Development Fund (EDF) for the development of local companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This will support the efforts that are undertaken at the enterprise level to upgrade capabilities, automate 	Page: 28 processes and internationalise.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In addition, as part of the S$4.5 billion Industry Transformation Programme announced in Budget 2016, the Government will develop customised roadmaps for key industries.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is really what the Industry Transformation Maps are about.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Each roadmap will comprise a growth and competitiveness plan, supported by strategies to upgrade productivity, develop skills, promote technology adoption and innovation, and help our companies expand overseas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about falling private investments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Attracting investments remains a key part of our strategy to grow the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The investment commitments that EDB has secured for fixed asset investments (FAI) have moderated from S$12.1 billion in 2013 to S$11.5 billion in 2015.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is partly due to the uncertain global economic conditions, but it is also a reflection of our targeted approach towards attracting projects that are more consistent with our stage of economic development, manpower policies and international commitments on carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Companies generally understand and accept these constraints, which are by no means unique to Singapore, and have been supportive of our push towards productivity-driven growth.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Re-investments from the existing base of companies have focused on increasing productivity through the adoption of automation technologies and upskilling of the workforce.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In addition, EDB continues to harness investor interest in the growth markets of Asia and ASEAN to establish "Homes", that is, headquarters that comprise top decision-makers and differentiating competencies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These initiatives do not always entail large FAIs but they create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan asked if there have been difficulties filling jobs created via EDB's investment commitments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At the project level, EDB works closely with the companies to meet their projected job commitments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And this includes partnering our academic institutions and industry to ensure that Singaporeans are equipped with the appropriate skillsets to take up the diverse range of jobs that are on offer.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At the same time, our industry transformation efforts, which I have described, will also support sustainable job creation in the medium term in both new and existing industries.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Many of these jobs, and others in sectors like education and healthcare, are suitable not just for new entrants to the job market but also for mature workers seeking a new career.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Minister for Manpower will be elaborating on our efforts and measures to help workers adapt and secure these job opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is critical that our companies stand ready to embrace new technologies and business models and that our workers stay open to 	Page: 29 learning new skills and capabilities in order to take on new or redesigned jobs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On its part, the Government is firmly committed to supporting our workers and companies through this transformation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And he explained that the targeted approach actually led to the decline.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In light of the economic transformation and the cyclical headwinds, the data show also, in terms of declining foreign manufacturing investments over the past two and half years or so, I am a bit concerned on that part and I am wondering what the Government's view is in terms of declining foreign manufacturing investments, particularly because the job creation in the manufacturing side would probably create a bit more volume than that on the services side.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And what would be the Government's strategy in terms of the declining foreign manufacturing investments in light of the decline in EDB's foreign investment commitments over the next five to 10 years?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, it is a different order of magnitude.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, it is no longer just about investing in fixed assets, plants, equipment and doing manufacturing in the conventional sense that we understand.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, manufacturing has got a very significant complementary aspect.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What it basically means is that traditional manufacturers are also embarking on very different service-oriented models.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We understand Rolls Royce to be a company that sells engines for aircraft.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But Rolls Royce is increasingly moving towards a model where they sell power by the hour.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In other words, I do not sell you the engine but I sell you the power that drives the aircraft by the hour.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It may not always be reflected as an investment in manufacturing in our context, but, in terms of its impact on the economy and in terms of what we are doing for job creation, it remains absolutely valid.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, in a very general sense, manufacturing is changing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Having said that, even at the more traditional understanding of manufacturing, we continue to attract good investments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we continue to attract good quality manufacturing investments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the key is really to make sure that the investments that we attract are consistent with, first, as I have said earlier, our stage of development, because it is no point shoe-horning a manufacturer into our environment if it is not something that is sustainable in the medium to long-term.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Far better for us to target the sectors or the part of the value chain that can continue to operate in Singapore in a sustainable way and that will then drive economic growth and job creation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just a few days ago, there was a pharmaceutical research company that pulled out of Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be more companies pulling out of Singapore?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The second question is that, on the ground, there are quite a lot of retrenchments as well as pay cuts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is the Minister concerned with these and are there any measures to be taken soon?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think she is referring to the announcement about Novartis moving out their tropical disease research facility.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I do not want to go into the details of a specific company or what drives their decisions, but let me make a more general point.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: First of all, one should not read too much into individual cases because individual companies make decisions for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It could be because of internal restructuring; sometimes, it could be something as prosaic as a person in charge of that particular line of business deciding they want to run things in a different way.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And all these things have got knock-on effects in the way that business is restructured.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I would not want to extrapolate from that and draw broader conclusions about the viability, for example, in this case, of our pharmaceutical space.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, in the context of Singapore, we continue to attract good investments in this space.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We should not be complacent, but it is not something that should cause great alarm because it is in the context of one particular company making a decision on one particular aspect of its activity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The other point was about retrenchments, pay cuts and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think the Minister for Manpower will be addressing several of these points later.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But let me just make a more general point.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The real challenge for us is in ensuring that Singaporeans have the right skillsets in order to be able to take those jobs and run with it and develop new careers with it, in the case of those who are switching careers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, that is really a summary of the situation, and the Minister for Manpower will be able to give a far more detailed explanation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But I think that is a challenge because we all know about the slack in the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: My question, if I may, goes back to the last point that the Minister made, which is, with increasing job creation and the slack in the labour market, what are the challenges?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Have we seen what had happened in the last five years, for instance, where we had either been able to or not able to find a match between supply and demand of certain types of skilled manpower?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If I may clarify, the Member's question is whether we have been able to find appropriate manpower to fill the jobs, is that correct?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: First, I want to just restate the point I made earlier, Mdm Speaker, which is that EDB's efforts continue to generate jobs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are some sectors, other sectors where also there are jobs being created, for example, in education and healthcare.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are also sectors which are 	Page: 31 taking a bit of a hit because of external headwinds and, therefore, there is job decline there.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, you have to look at the economy as a whole.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is uneven, there are pockets where the opportunities exist for companies, for individuals.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are pockets where the environment and the circumstances are more challenging.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The point about whether we are able to find appropriate people, Singaporeans, to take up the jobs, this continues to be the key challenge because we are seeing major changes in the way various industries are running, because there is a lot more emphasis, and if I can just take one or two cases in point.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In the whole digital economy space, the importance of site security and having people who understand digital space and are able to work with data and do analytics and inform a company's business and marketing strategies, these are very essential skillsets in the new economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There is a global shortage of people in this sort of space.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we are creating opportunities and there are other sectors I can talk about.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There is always this issue of a skills mismatch, which is why we need to work on this on a few levels.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is on the one side; this is more pre-employment for new entrants.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But on the other side is really for the mature workers who are looking to switch careers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But they need to make the move, adapt, take up the relevant skills training and adjustment in order to be able to participate in the new business.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we have seen examples of people doing that.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In the bio-pharmaceutical company that I visited, I saw an individual who was in his late 40s, worked in China in the electronics sector and came back because the company terminated his employment.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: He came back, he decided he wanted to make a switch, he got into the biopharmaceutical space, he got the training through WDA – and I think it is the Professional Conversion Programme – and now heads the unit there or certain aspects of production.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Individual stories, but demonstrating that the larger strategy can work and we need the individuals to step up and benefit fully from our programmes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And related to that, whether as these companies fail, are we at risk of permanently losing these capabilities – engineering and economic capabilities, for example, for the oil and gas sector – the contracting capabilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And whether the Government will come up with sector-specific measures to help these industries and sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the Industry Transformation Map, whether you want to activate this early to help these companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I think the data the Member looked at was 	Page: 32 for September.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I think this has got something also to do and there is some explanation there about some technical treatment.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I would urge Members to check it out and maybe file a PQ to get further clarification.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the first point I am making is that in the first two quarters of this year, rather than negative, there has actually been positive enterprise formation, at least based on the data we get from ACRA.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think the more important point the Member is raising is really whether we have a concern in terms of what is happening on the ground, in terms of companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Enterprise formation, we know some companies form SPVs, there is restructuring, these things happen all the time.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They do not necessarily reflect or affect what is happening on the ground in terms of actual business and jobs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I would say that, if I go back to the point I made earlier, there is a diversity; if you look at the landscape, it is variegated.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Some sectors are doing well or reasonably well, others are having a hard time.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Even within the sectors that are challenged, there are companies that are thriving because they have been able to adapt, or they have been able to find a niche and they are doing well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The fact of the matter is that it is an uneven terrain.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not so much about having a broad-brush general programme or strategy because that is just going to be wasteful and some would argue that the natural business cycle should be allowed to take its course so that there is some appropriate consolidation and re-channelling of resources at the economy level.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are mindful there are certain sectors or industries where we do need to be very careful, that we do not, in the process, lose core capabilities that have been built up over a long period of time.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Therefore, in those sorts of very specific areas, we are tracking it and we are working on ideas as to how we can do this in a way that does not become so interventionist that it distorts the market, but it minimises the loss of capabilities, which we need to preserve in order to sustain the competitiveness of our companies in those sectors, especially when the situation improves.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Minister spoke about transformations of the various industries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One feedback I often get from the industries is: how do they align with some of these strategies and sub-strategies because a lot of times the Ministry talks about strategies in very broad terms?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: From a sector-specific agenda, would the Ministry be sharing specific sector strategies, whether certain sectors will be defocused and others ramped up.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think what the industry is looking for is guidance so that that also helps in terms of manpower deployment and transformation, for example, where do they align to?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry be sharing its sub-strategies in a more detailed manner?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have already announced a couple of them.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One is in food services and another is for retail.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There will be progressively more of these programmes that will be announced and shared.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These programmes go into a great deal of detail in terms of the productivity, innovation, internationalisation and manpower aspects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Many of the programmes that we have are being, at the backend, integrated and channelled along these lines.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For the businesses, in order to understand and navigate the space, the first thing I would say is we will definitely be communicating this not just through major announcements but 	Page: 33 it will be percolated down through the industry associations and various other channels.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Second, even if the larger transformation plan may not be entirely relevant for a particular business, what they need to do – I am talking about the SMEs in particular – is to get in touch with one of our SME Centres, quite a number of which are now on the ground, through our various chambers and trade associations, or through the trade association and industry association members, or directly with SPRINGSingapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Then, the dialogue can start on what is appropriate in terms of the companies' own plans and strategies, and how some of the programmes that we have can assist them.
